To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the development of PKDL after treatment of kalla‐azar is associated with the acquisition of Leishmaniasis‐reactivity by peripheral blood T cells; (2) this reactivity is associated with the production of IFN‐γ; (3) the reactivity is specific for Leishmania and not cross‐reactive with other antigens.
PKDL develops in kala‐azar patients after treatment as Leishmania reactive T cells start to be detected in the peripheral blood.

PKDL develops in Sudanese patients after treatment for visceral leishmaniais (kala-azar) as Leishmania-reactive T cells start circulating in peripheral blood in numbers that can be detected in in vitro assays.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of PKDL, which is a neglected tropical disease that affects millions of people in the developing world.
the immunological mechanisms of disease progression from visceral leishmanisis to PKDL.
the development of a vaccine for visceral leishamaniasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PKDL develops as a result of a delayed immune response to Leishmaniasis antigens.
the development of PKDL is a consequence of the immune response against Leishmania parasites, which have persisted in the skin after treatment of visceral kala‐azar.
PKDL develops in patients who have a high Leishmania antigen reactivity and who have been successfully treated for visceral leischmaniasis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of PKDL is a consequence of an immune response to the Leishmania parasites that have survived in the dermis after the treatment for kala‐azar.
PKDL develops in Sudanese patients after treatment of kalahazar when Leishmania‐specific T cells start to be detected in peripheral blood in in vitroblood assays.
PKDL is the consequence of an immune response to Leishmaniainfection, which has been reactivated after treatment of visceral disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Leishmania‐induced IFN‐γ responses are a reliable marker for predicting the development of PKDL in kala‐azar.
the development of PKDL in Sudan is associated with a Leishmania antigen–specific T‐cell response.
the presence of a Leishmania‐specific T‐cell response is not sufficient to cause PKDL, and that the immune response needs to be able to reach the skin.
